newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico's mark bond to refinance maturing debt.
newsitem.headline: Mexico's mark bond to refinance maturing debt.

text.p: The Mexican government will use its latest bond issue -- a 12-year 1.5 billion German mark ($915 million) placement made on Tuesday -- to refinance part of its debt coming due this year, the Finance Ministry said.
The refinancing will help extend the term structure of the government's external debt, a key part of Mexico's debt strategy.

"It is important to underline that the (1997) maturing debt corresponds to issues placed in 1995 at terms of 15 months and two years, which are being refinanced at a 12-year term," the ministry said in a statement.
The spread on the bond came in on the low side of expectations, yielding 8.295 percent, or 264 basis points over comparable U.S. Treasuries.
The issue was originally seen as yielding 260 to 280 basis points more than the new German 10-year, 6.0 percent government bond.
Strong demand for high-yielding mark paper helped bump up the amount that Mexico issued and to push down the yield, analysts said.
Mexico originally planned to issue a bond worth only one billion marks ($609.3 million), but like other recent Mexico debt issues, the size was increased on the heavy demand.
The federal government only has $1.4 billion in maturing market debt this year, but officials have said they are also considering buying back outstanding Aztec Brady bonds.

Mexico tapped the German mark market last year when it placed an eight-year one billion mark ($675 million) structured issue that was later bumped up by another 500 million marks. The issue paid 304 basis points more than U.S. Treasuries.
It has now placed debt denominated in marks at terms of five, seven and eight years, in addition to the latest 12-year bond.
With crucial mid-term elections planned this July, Mexico has rushed to place issues before what could prove to be a period of intense political volatility.
Last week, the federal government also placed a 10-year 500 billion Italian lira bond, worth about $310 million, aimed at refinancing maturing debt in 1997.
